title: Martin Freeman & Jack Lowden in The Fifth Step - review

Jack Louden is Luca, a newly recovering addict nearing the fifth step of the AA program. Martin Freeman is James, an older mentor who's been through it and offers his experience to the younger man. At first, Luca is a man who needs help. He doesn't know what to do or where to turn once he's given up drink. And Jack Louden gives Luke a tearyeyed desperation as when he says, "I think I might be an incel." James offers wisdom and advice, but whatever crutch Luca reaches for, like a bouncing puppy with wideeyed hope, James moves him on. Don't go to the pub. Don't masturbate. Don't have an affair with a married woman. Don't believe in Jesus. These are some of the funniest moments as when sexist Luca speaks in a filthy way about women without seeing that that could be a problem. And meanwhile, an exasperated James makes rye often cynical comments. But it turns out that neither of them are fully to be believed, and the two actors excel at conveying and concealing layers of truth. At first, Martin Freeman is smiling, firm in his pronouncements, and with a gimlet eye on Luca. But there's something about his controlling manner and his pointing finger that make you wonder about him even from the start. The meetings between the two continue and Luca gains in self-esteem until they reach the fifth step, which is confession about the harm their addiction may have done. It's then that we see what happens when faith is exploited and trust breaks down. The newly more confident Lucer challenges his mentor as revelations about James's contradictory instructions and hypocritical behavior emerge. And when that happens, James starts to break down with an aggressive defensiveness that includes nasty insults and actual truly shocking violence near the end, which brought a gasp from the audience. questions about the nature and abuse of authority come to the four already primed by earlier references to abuse of children by priests. I did feel the ending was rather silly and soft and a bit sentimental after such searing black comedy and I could have done without so many references to the importance of spiritual belief even if there are some good jokes about it.
